prompt: Let $m,d$ be positive integers, with $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and $[d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}$. A graph $G$ has a tree-model $(T,S)$: the leaves of the rooted tree $T$ are $V(G)$, all at depth $d$, and $S\subseteq[m]^2\times[d]$ is symmetric in its first two coordinates. Distinct leaves $u,v$ have colours $i,j\in[m]$ and distance $2\ell$, where $\ell\in[d]$. How is their adjacency defined?

answers.explanation: The signature uses the two leaf colours and half their tree distance. With all leaves at depth $d$, this is equivalent to using their least common ancestor’s depth.
Distinct leaves are not joined by a tree edge in these models. Graph adjacency is interpreted from the signature.
Equal-colour pairs can be adjacent or nonadjacent depending on the signature and distance.
Sibling leaves need not be adjacent, and leaves farther apart may be adjacent.
The third signature coordinate ranges over half-distances, not full tree distances.
Here the signature was indexed by half-distance. Using least-common-ancestor depth requires translating the signature too.
This uses the complementary signature and produces the complement graph.
This forgets the actual distance and may add edges intended only for other levels.
Adjacency at the actual level does not require adjacency at every possible level.
Cross-colour adjacency is its own signature entry; it need not follow from either same-colour entry.

sources.title: Ganian et al. — Shrub-depth: Capturing Height of Dense Graphs, §§2–4
